'''Carlo Fortunato Pietro Ponti Sr.''' {{post-nominals|post-noms=[[Order of Merit of the Italian Republic|Cavaliere di Gran Croce OMRI]]}} (11 December 1912 – 10 January 2007) was an Italian [[film producer]] with more than 140 productions to his credit. Along with [[Dino De Laurentiis]], he is credited with reinvigorating  and popularizing [[Italian cinema]] post-World War II,<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Lyman,AP|first1=Eric J.|last2=Lyman|first2=Eric J.|last3=AP|date=2007-01-11|title=Italian producer Carlo Ponti dies at 94|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/italian-producer-carlo-ponti-dies-127710/|access-date=2021-10-27|website=The Hollywood Reporter|language=en-US}}</ref> producing some of the country's most acclaimed and financially-successful films of the 1950s and 1960s.

Ponti worked with many of the most important directors of Italian cinema of the era, including [[Federico Fellini]], [[Michelangelo Antonioni]], and [[Vittorio De Sica]], as well as many international directors such as [[Agnès Varda]] and [[David Lean]]. He helped launch the career of his wife, international film star [[Sophia Loren]]. He won the [[Academy Award for Best Foreign-Language Film]] for ''[[La Strada]]'' (1954) and was nominated for [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] for producing [[Doctor Zhivago (film)|''Doctor Zhivago'']] (1965). In 1996, he was appointed as a [[Knight Grand Cross of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Le onorificenze della Repubblica Italiana|url=https://www.quirinale.it/onorificenze/insigniti/11599|access-date=2021-10-27|website=www.quirinale.it}}</ref>

==Early life==
Ponti was born in [[Magenta, Lombardy]], where his grandfather had been mayor of the city. Ponti studied law at the [[University of Milan]]. He joined his father's law firm in [[Milan]] and became involved in the film business through negotiating contracts.<ref name="independent">{{cite news| last =Exshaw| first =John| title =Carlo Ponti| newspaper =[[The Independent]]| date =12 January 2007| url =http://news.independent.co.uk/people/obituaries/article2144032.ece| access-date =2007-01-12| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20070219203402/http://news.independent.co.uk/people/obituaries/article2144032.ece| archive-date =19 February 2007}}</ref>

==Career==
===Early films===
Ponti attempted to establish a film industry in Milan in 1940 and produced [[Mario Soldati]]'s ''[[Piccolo mondo antico (film)|Piccolo mondo antico]]'' there, starring [[Alida Valli]], in her first notable role. The film dealt with the [[Second Italian War of Independence|Italian struggle against the Austrians]] for the inclusion of northeastern Italy into the [[Kingdom of Sardinia|Kingdom of Italy]] during the [[Italian unification|Risorgimento]]. The film was successful, because it was easy to see "the Austrians as Germans" during World War II.<ref name="nytimes">{{cite news| last =Martin|first =Douglas
| title =Carlo Ponti |newspaper =[[The New York Times]]  | date =11 January 2007| url =https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/11/movies/11ponti.html| access-date =2007-01-14  }}</ref>  As a result, Ponti was briefly jailed for undermining relations with [[Nazi Germany]].<ref name="Kansas">{{cite news| title =Movie Producer Carlo Ponti Dies| newspaper =Kansas City Star
| date =2007-01-10|url=http://www.kansascity.com/mld/kansascity/entertainment/gossip/16426212.htm|access-date = 2007-01-14 }}</ref>

Ponti accepted an offer from [[Riccardo Gualino]]'s [[Lux Film]] in [[Rome]] in 1941.<ref name="guardian">{{cite news
|last =Lane  | first =John Francis|title =Carlo Ponti| newspaper =[[The Guardian]]
|date =11 January 2007|url =http://film.guardian.co.uk/obituaries/0,,1987651,00.html
|access-date =2007-01-14}}</ref> He made ''[[Giacomo the Idealist]]'' (1943), ''[[A Yank in Rome]]'' (1946), ''[[To Live in Peace]]'' (1947), ''[[The White Primrose]]'' (1948), ''[[Prelude to Madness]]'' (1948) and ''[[Hey Boy (film)|Hey Boy]]'' (1948).

Ponti produced some films starring [[Gina Lollobrigida]]: ''[[Alarm Bells]]'' (1949), ''[[The White Line (1950 film)|The White Line]]'' (1950), ''[[A Dog's Life (1950 film)|A Dog's Life]]'' (1950). ''[[Her Favourite Husband]]'' (1950) was a British-Italian co production with Jean Kent.  He made a number of comedies including ''[[Figaro Here, Figaro There]]'' (1950), ''[[Toto the Third Man]]'' (1951) and ''[[Toto in Color]]'' (1952), with [[Totò]], plus ''[[The Knight Has Arrived!]]'' (1951), ''[[The Piano Tuner Has Arrived]]'' (1952) and ''[[The Steamship Owner]]'' (1951) with [[Walter Chiari]]. Ponti alternated this with more serious material such as ''[[Europe '51]]'' (1952) from [[Roberto Rossellini]], ''[[Brothers of Italy (film)|Brothers of Italy]]'' (1952), ''[[Lieutenant Giorgio]]'' (1953), and ''[[Easy Years]]'' (1953). ''[[The Unfaithfuls]]'' (1953) reunited Ponti with Lollobrigida, while ''[[Neapolitan Carousel]]'' (1954) won the International Prize at Cannes.

===International breakthrough and Sophia Loren===
In 1954 Ponti had his greatest artistic success with the production of [[Federico Fellini]]'s ''[[La strada (film)|La strada]]''. However, Fellini denied Ponti's role in its success and said that "''La Strada'' was made in spite of Ponti and [[Dino De Laurentiis|De Laurentiis]]".<ref name="guardian" />  Along with a Toto comedy ''[[The Doctor of the Mad]]'' (1954) he and de Laurentiis produced an international film, ''[[Mambo (film)|Mambo]]'' (1954) directed by Robert Rossen. There was ''[[An American in Rome]]'' (1955) with [[Alberto Sordi]] and ''[[The Gold of Naples]]'' (1954) with a young Sophia Loren.

Loren was the female lead in Ponti's ''[[Attila (1954 film)|Attila]]'' (1954), a biopic of Attila the Hun with Anthony Quinn that became a big box office success. Loren was in ''[[The Miller's Beautiful Wife]]'' (1955), a comedy.

Ponti and de Laurentiis made the epic war film ''[[War and Peace (1956 film)|War and Peace]]'' (1956). In June 1956 his partnership with De Laurentiis ended after more than eighty films over six years.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Variety|url=https://archive.org/details/variety203-1956-06/page/n82/mode/1up?q=%22carlo+ponti%22|title=Ponti-De Laurentiis Partnership Ends|date=13 June 1956|page=20}}</ref>

Ponti continued to produce smaller movies for the Italian market such as ''[[The Railroad Man]]'' (1956), and ''[[Guendalina (film)|Guendalina]]'' (1957), but his focus was increasingly on bigger budgeted films aimed at the international market starring Loren: ''[[The Black Orchid (film)|The Black Orchid]]'' (1959) with Anthony Quinn, ''[[That Kind of Woman]]'' (1959) with Tab Hunter, ''[[Heller in Pink Tights]]'' (1960) with Quinn again, ''[[A Breath of Scandal]]'' (1960) with John Gavin. ''[[Two Women]]'' (1960), starring Loren and directed by Vittorio de Sica, was a huge success, winning Loren the Oscar.

===French films===
Ponti produced a series of movies in France: ''[[Lola (1961 film)|Lola]]'' (1961) starred Anouk Aimee, ''[[A Woman Is a Woman]]'' (1961) directed by [[Jean-Luc Godard]], ''[[Léon Morin, Priest]]'' (1961) from [[Jean-Pierre Melville]] starring [[Jean Paul Belmondo]], ''[[Cléo from 5 to 7]]'' (1962) from [[Agnès Varda]], ''[[Le Doulos]]'' (1962) with Belmondo, ''[[Landru (film)|Landru]]'' (1962), plus ''[[The Carabineers]]'' (1963) and ''[[Contempt (film)|Contempt]]'' (1963) from Godard.

Ponti continued to make movies in Italy, notably ''[[Boccaccio '70]]'' (1962), ''[[Redhead (1962 film)|Redhead]]'' (1962), ''[[The Empty Canvas]]'' (1962), ''[[Break Up (1965 film)|Break Up]]'' (1965) and two with Loren, ''[[Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow]]'' (1963) and ''[[Marriage Italian Style]]'' (1964).

===MGM===
Ponti produced his most popular and financially successful film, ''[[Doctor Zhivago (1965 film)|Doctor Zhivago]],'' in 1965; the movie was directed by [[David Lean]] and made by MGM. Also for MGM Ponti produced ''[[Operation Crossbow (film)|Operation Crossbow]]'' (1965), a war film with Loren, ''[[The Girl and the General]]'' (1967) with Rod Steiger, ''[[Ghosts – Italian Style]]'' (1967), and three notable films with [[Michelangelo Antonioni]], ''[[Blowup]]'' in 1966, ''[[Zabriskie Point (film)|Zabriskie Point]]'' in 1970 and ''[[The Passenger (1975 film)|The Passenger]]'' in 1974.

He made ''[[The 10th Victim]]'' (1965), and some films for Paramount, ''[[Smashing Time]]'' (1967) ''[[Diamonds for Breakfast (film)|Diamonds for Breakfast]]'' (1968).

===Later career===
Ponti's later movies included ''[[The Priest's Wife]]'' (1970) with Loren, ''[[What? (film)|What?]]'' (1972) from Roman Polanski, ''[[Giordano Bruno (film)|Giordano Bruno]]'' (1973), ''[[Torso (1973 film)|Torso]]'' (1973) a gallo with Suzy Kendall, ''[[Dirty Weekend (1973 film)|Dirty Weekend]]'' (1973) with Oliver Reed, ''[[Mr. Hercules Against Karate]]'' (1973), ''[[Flesh for Frankenstein]]'' (1974), ''[[The Voyage (1974 film)|The Voyage]]'' (1974) with Loren, ''[[Sex Pot (1975 film)|Sex Pot]]'' (1975) with Loren and Mastroinanni, ''[[L'Infermiera]]'' (1975) with Ursula Andress, and ''[[Down and Dirty (film)|Down and Dirty]]'' (1977),

His final credits included ''[[The Cassandra Crossing]]'' (1977), an international co production starring Loren, and ''[[A Special Day]]'' (1977) with Mastroianni and Loren.

==Personal life==
===Marriages===
In 1946, he married Giuliana Fiastri with whom he had a daughter, Guendalina,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm1731110/bio|title=Guendalina Ponti|website=IMDb|access-date=2020-03-21}}</ref> in 1951, and a son, Alex,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm0690637/bio|title=Alex Ponti|website=IMDb|access-date=2020-03-21}}</ref> in 1953.<ref name="times">{{cite news |title =Carlo Ponti
|newspaper =[[The Times]]|date =11 January 2007
|url =http://www.timesonline.co.uk/article/0,,3-2540805,00.html
|access-date =2007-01-12 | location=London}}{{dead link|date=September 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> While serving as a judge in a beauty contest in 1951, Ponti met a minor actress named [[Sophia Loren|Sofia Lazzaro]] (real name Sofia Costanza Brigida Villani Scicolone). He subsequently cast her in films such as ''[[Anna (1951 film)|Anna]]'' (1951). In 1952, his friend Goffredo Lombardo, head of production at [[Titanus]], changed Lazzaro's name to [[Sophia Loren]].

Five years later, Ponti obtained a [[Mexican divorce]] from his first wife and married Sophia Loren by [[Proxy marriage|proxy]]. Divorce was still forbidden in Italy, and he was informed that were he to return there, he would be charged with bigamy, and Loren would be charged with "[[concubinage]]".

Ponti co-produced several films in Hollywood starring Loren, establishing her fame. In 1960, he and Loren returned to Italy and when summoned to court, denied being married. In 1962, they had the marriage annulled, after which Ponti arranged with his first wife, Giuliana, that the three of them move to France (which at that time allowed divorce) and become French citizens. In 1965, Giuliana Ponti divorced her husband, allowing Ponti to marry Loren in 1966 in a civil wedding in [[Sèvres, France|Sèvres]].<ref name="independent" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://marriage.about.com/od/entertainmen1/p/sophialoren.htm|title=Sophia Loren and Carlo Ponti Marriage Profile|publisher=About|author=Sheri & Bob Stritof|access-date=2008-06-05|archive-date=2016-08-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160810051502/http://marriage.about.com/od/entertainmen1/p/sophialoren.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tvfanforums.net/index.php?showtopic=17345|title=Italian Producer Carlo Ponti|publisher=Associated Press|quote=archived at TV Fan Forums|date=January 2007|access-date=2008-06-05|archive-date=2012-10-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121003221032/http://www.tvfanforums.net/index.php?showtopic=17345|url-status=dead}}</ref> They later became French citizens after their application was approved by then-French Prime Minister [[Georges Pompidou]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/story/carlo-ponti-husband-to-sophia-loren-dead-at-94|title=Carlo Ponti, Husband to Sophia Loren, Dead at 94|work=[[Fox News]]|date=January 10, 2007|access-date=2010-10-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130904200836/http://www.foxnews.com/story/0,2933,242764,00.html|archive-date=2013-09-04|url-status=live}}</ref>

Ponti and Loren had two sons:
* [[Carlo Ponti (conductor)|Carlo Ponti Jr.]] (born 29 December 1968)
* [[Edoardo Ponti]] (born 6 January 1973)

Their daughters-in-law are [[Sasha Alexander]] and Andrea Meszaros.<ref>{{cite news|author=Davies, Lizzy |date= October 24, 2013|title=Sophia Loren wins tax case after 40 years|work= The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://www.life.com/image/51321373|title=Carlo Ponti Jr. Weds in St. Stephen's Basilica|magazine=Life|date=September 18, 2004|access-date=December 10, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110610222019/http://www.life.com/image/51321373|archive-date=June 10, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> They have four grandchildren.

Loren remained married to Ponti until his death on 10 January 2007 of pulmonary complications.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hellomagazine.com/film/2007/01/10/carlo-ponte-loren|title=Sophia Loren's Husband Carlo Ponti Passes Away|work=Hello|date=10 January 2007|access-date=10 December 2010}}</ref>

===Kidnapping attempts===
Two unsuccessful attempts were made to kidnap Ponti in 1975, including one involving an attack on his car with gunfire.<ref name="independent" />

===Smuggling charges===
He was tried ''in absentia'' in 1979 for smuggling money and works of art abroad, fined 22 billion [[Italian lira|lire]], and sentenced to four years in prison. Ponti did not attend the hearing, as his French nationality made him immune from extradition. He was finally cleared of the charges in 1990.<ref name="independent" />

==Art collection==
Ponti owned works by, among others, [[Pablo Picasso|Picasso]], [[Georges Braque]], [[Pierre-Auguste Renoir|Renoir]], [[René Magritte]] (including his ''Lumière du pole'' from 1927), [[Salvador Dalí]], [[Henry Moore]] (including his ''Figure'' from 1933), [[Barbara Hepworth]], [[Giorgio de Chirico]] and [[Canaletto]]. His collection was renowned for containing ten works by [[Francis Bacon (artist)|Francis Bacon]]. These included examples from his early Van Gogh series, triptychs, self-portraits and pope paintings, which were rarely publicised or lent to public exhibitions. In 1977 the Bacon paintings, then valued at an estimated $6.7 million, were seized and turned over by the Italian government to the [[Pinacoteca di Brera]] in Milan; thirty-three sketches by [[George Grosz]] went to a museum in [[Caserta]].<ref>Sam Kashner (March 2012), [http://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2012/03/sophia-loren-201203 Sophia’s Choices] ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]''.</ref> When Ponti reached a deal with the Italian government and was cleared of the charges brought against him in 1990, he regained possession of 230 confiscated paintings.<ref>Nancy Collins (January 1991), [http://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/features/1991/01/sophia-loren-199101 Sophia] ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]''.</ref> At some point, the collection is said to have been split between Ponti and Loren.<ref name="telegraph.co.uk">Colin Gleadell (January 30, 2007), [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/art/3662858/Art-sales-Sophia-Lorens-slice-of-Bacon.html Art sales: Sophia Loren's slice of Bacon] ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]''.</ref>

Over the years, several works have been sold privately. In 2006 two Bacon paintings that had previously been in the Ponti collection were exhibited in an exhibition at the [[Gagosian Gallery]] in London. One, a vertical composition of four self-portraits, had already been sold to the American collector [[Steven A. Cohen]]. In 2007 another pope painting by Bacon, sold by Ponti in 1991, was sold in a private deal brokered by [[Acquavella Galleries]] in New York for more than £15 million. That same year, ''Study for Portrait II'' (1956) was consigned by Loren at [[Christie's]];<ref name="telegraph.co.uk"/> it was auctioned for the record price of £14.2 million ($27.5 million).<ref>[https://archive.today/20120709021439/http://in.artinfo.com/news/story/24271/modern-art-sales-fetch-european-record Modern Art Sales Fetch European Record] ''ARTINFO'', November 30, 2007.</ref>

==Death==
Carlo Ponti Sr died on January 10th, 2007 in [[Geneva]], Switzerland, after being hospitalized for 10 days for pulmonary complications. Carlo Ponti  Sr was 94 years old.<ref name="nytimes" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/carlo-ponti-431602.html|title=Carlo Ponti|date=11 January 2007|website=The Independent}}</ref> He was survived by his daughter Guendalina (b. 1951), and his son Alessandro (b. 1953) from his first marriage; and by his second wife, Sophia Loren, and their sons [[Carlo Ponti Jr.|Carlo]] (b. 1968) and [[Edoardo Ponti]] (b. 1973).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2007/jan/11/guardianobituaries.italy|title=Obituary: Carlo Ponti|website=[[TheGuardian.com]] |date=11 January 2007}}</ref>

His body rests in the family tomb in [[Magenta, Lombardy]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wistv.com/story/5932761/italian-producer-carlo-ponti-buried|title=Italian producer Carlo Ponti buried|website=wistv.com|date=13 January 2007 }}</ref>
